bib.title: Chapter 11. Conclusions and the Future (Reinforcement Learning: Industrial Applications of Intelligent Agents)

question: What practical tips for framing, training, evaluating, deploying and debugging RL apply in industry, and where is RL heading?
contributions: Tips and tricks for RL practice

results.claim: Most RL failures come from the problem being unsuited to RL, not the algorithm; MountainCar-v0 is an exploration and credit-assignment problem.
results.quote:
The main reason why RL methods fail is not because the algorithm isn’t
good enough, but because the problem isn’t suited to being solved in this
way.

limits: Opinion and experience chapter; no experiments, no quantitative evidence of its own.
Market and timing predictions (RL commodity in up to 10 years, 2023 Gartner forecast) are from 2020 and have dated.
Research directions predate offline RL maturation, LLM-based RL and RLHF.
Cited sources are web posts and talks (Reddit thread, Schulman talk, Rahtz blog), not peer reviewed.
practices: Frame the problem first: visualize a random policy and try the task yourself as the agent; if neither finds viable behaviour, RL is unlikely to help (Framing the Problem).
Build baselines in order: random agent, cross-entropy method, then simple Q-learning or policy gradient, treating each as an experiment (Framing the Problem).
Simplify the state, action space, goal and reward; replace sparse rewards with smooth ones such as distance to goal and remove outliers and discontinuities (Framing the Problem).
Add working memory (e.g. recurrent networks) only if states must be visited in a specific order, and check first whether a shortcut action removes the need (Framing the Problem).
Consider solving disparate skills independently before using hierarchical RL (Framing the Problem).
Rescale observations to zero mean and unit standard deviation (rolling statistics or observed limits) and decorrelate them with z-transform, PCA or differencing (Your Data).
Monitor reward distributions, inputs, value predictions, gradients, action entropy and KL divergence (Your Data).
Increase the time between actions (frame skipping) to stabilize and speed up training (Your Data).
Develop against a range of environments, use multiple seeds and test hyperparameter sensitivity to avoid overfitting the algorithm to one environment (Training).
Use learning rate schedules rather than a fixed rate (Training).
Compare algorithms by plotting curves over many seeds; if there is no clear gap, run more seeds or distrust the result (Evaluation).
Evaluate with deterministic policy and disabled exploration, but consider keeping stochasticity in the real environment if the optimal policy may drift (Evaluation).
Prefer less code and off-the-shelf components; deployment needs significant software engineering and good architecture (Deployment, Debugging).

For debugging, log observations, actions and rewards, plot the value function over states and time, start with a linear or single-layer network, and get fixed seeds and single threading working before scaling (Monitoring for Debugging).
Get a practical problem, ideally at work, rather than toy examples (Next Steps).
